result:
On the morning the clocks stopped, nobody noticed at first.

The baker pulled six loaves from the oven and found them pale. He put them back for five minutes, then ten, then stood with the oven door open until the heat stung his face. The loaves stayed pale. Across the street, a woman waited for the kettle to boil. Her tea went cold around the leaves.

By noon, people had begun to gather in the square. Every clock showed 8:17. Watches, phones, the brass face above the bank: all of them. The sun had moved, and the shadows had moved with it. Children had grown hungry. Whatever was wrong, it wasn't time itself.

Mrs. Vale arrived carrying her grandfather's pocket watch. It had no hands. Her grandfather had taken them out years ago, she said, after the watch began losing minutes that never turned up again.

“That doesn't help us,” said the mayor.

“It might,” said Mrs. Vale. “He's still alive.”

They found him at home, asleep in an armchair beside a cold fireplace. Mr. Vale was ninety-six and disliked visitors, but he listened while the mayor explained. Then he asked for his coat.

“There used to be someone who looked after the clocks,” he said as they walked. “His name was Harlan. He could hear a bad gear from the street. After he died, I tried to keep them running. They're old, most of them.”

At the square, he opened the bank clock with a key he had kept for forty years. Inside, the pendulum hung motionless. He gave it a push. It swung once, then stopped.

Mr. Vale lowered himself onto the steps and examined the works laid out beside him. A few people stayed to watch. Others went home to make supper without knowing when supper ought to be. The baker brought out the pale loaves. They were cooked through and tasted fine.

Toward evening, Mr. Vale found a broken tooth on a gear no bigger than a coin. The mayor sent someone for the clockmaker in the next town, but it was too late for him to come that night. Mr. Vale set the gear on a handkerchief and said there was nothing more to do until morning.

The sun went down. People lit lamps and went to bed. Some slept badly; others slept better than they had in years.

The clockmaker arrived the next day with a box of parts. By lunchtime the bank clock was ticking again. Its hands still pointed to 8:17, so the mayor asked what time they should set it to. No one was quite sure. They settled on twelve, because the sun was high and everyone was ready to eat.

For a while, the town was half a day out of step with everywhere else. Deliveries came unexpectedly. Calls were missed. The mayor bought a radio, and within a week all the clocks agreed with it.

But the baker kept one of the pale loaves on a shelf behind his counter. It hardened there, slowly, while customers came in to buy bread. When anyone asked about it, he told them how he had stood at the oven waiting for five minutes to pass, and how long it had taken him to open the door and look.
